newsitem.title: UK: FEATURE-UK firms shape up as rebel shareholders show teeth. [CORRECTED 17:50 GMT]
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-UK firms shape up as rebel shareholders show teeth. [CORRECTED 17:50 GMT]

text.p: Nobody used to listen when Britain's activist shareholders called for "green" and socially-responsible corporate policies.
Fellow shareholders treated them with scorn at annual meetings. Company boards dismissed them as a nuisance.
But the tide has turned.

"You had the vigilante consumer and now you have the vigilante investor. It is the two of them together which is the most powerful combination," said Blair Palese, head of public relations at "green" cosmetics group Body Shop.
British blue-chip companies increasingly invite lobby groups to their offices, study their demands and even act on them.
The recent round of annual shareholders' meetings showed lobby groups such as Pirc, World Development Movement and Friends of the Earth have become forces to be reckoned with.
This trend was in evidence at British Petroleum Co Plc's shareholder meeting in April.

Following protests from various activist organisations, BP was moved to elaborately defend its human-rights record in Colombia (corrects from Bolivia) after allegations that it had colluded with death squads.
RTZ also paid heed to persistent activist pressure at its meeting this month.
After hiring a former head of environmentalist group Friends of the Earth as a consultant, the world's largest mining firm promised shareholders it would publish its first environmental report.
PRESSURE GROUPS CHANGE STRATEGY, BUY SHARES
Lobby groups which have criticised RTZ's environmental record in the past few years have changed their strategy as they realised little was to be gained from disturbing shareholder meetings.
"Campaigns have entered a new phase: there used to be demonstrations outside and there would be disturbances inside (the meetings)," said Aditi Sharma, campaigner of World Development Movement.
"Now we buy shares and talk to investors."
Most pressure group progress has undoubtedly been made with Shell.
For years, the oil giant ignored worldwide protests against its presence in South Africa during the apartheid era.
But it changed tack after Greenpeace's landmark victory in 1994 when the protest group forced Shell to abandon plans to sink the Brent Spar oil storage platform.
Greenpeace later acknowledged its campaign was based on faulty data on the level of oil left on the platform.
Subsequent changes in Shell's corporate policy started to become visible this year.
In February, Shell revised its statement of business principles, which now explicitly sets out its support for fundamental human rights.
In addition, the company -- one of the world's biggest -- published its first worldwide health, safety and environment report last week.
REBELS SAY SHELL HAS MET MANY DEMANDS

Rebel shareholders, led by investment advisory service Pirc, say many of their demands have now been met, though the annual meeting rejected a resolution for an external audit of the Anglo-Dutch company's environmental record.

Pirc said it was not disappointed by the rejection, as Shell said it backed such an audit in principle and had only urged shareholders to reject the motion because it felt there was no consensus yet on the criteria to carry out an independent review.
Pirc ascribes recent activist successes to growing fears among investors that failing to pay attention to the environment now may backfire in the form of damage claims later.
Pirc joint managing director Alan MacDougall also cites increased pressure from insurance firms on other companies to act "greener" to limit the risk of future litigation.
"Insurers are no longer prepared to bail companies out in relation to risks incurred from using unsustainable production processes," he said.
